newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine roadblocks lifted as government offers aid.
newsitem.headline: Argentine roadblocks lifted as government offers aid.

text.p: Impoverished protesters in the northwestern Argentine province of Jujuy lifted roadblocks on Saturday and accepted provincial government offers of 12,000 new jobs, after several days of negotiation.
Church mediators announced the agreement to end the protest, the state-owned Telam news agency reported.

The roadblocks were the latest in a wave of protests against poverty and unemployment in Argentina, which started in April among teachers and oil workers in Patagonia and spread to the northern provinces of Salta and Jujuy and the central province of Cordoba.
Over 100 people were injured in clashes between the Jujuy protesters and police last week.
The protests rattled the government, and the Roman Catholic Church and the International Monetary Fund expressed concern about Argentina's chronic social problems.
President Carlos Menem said on Saturday that unemployment does not justify the protests sweeping poorer parts of the country but promised federal funds to create jobs.

"Unemployment cannot be converted into a matter of social agitation and discontent, nor into a matter for the courts with excesses and roadblocks and extremist attitudes," wrote Menem in an article carried by Telam news agency, "This president, besides guaranteeing social justice, must fundamentally guarantee public order."
But he promised the creation of a "Promotion and Development Body" to create jobs and attempt to resolve the causes of the protests.

"The repeated episodes disturbing public order make it necessary to address the problems by creating a network of protection in critical areas," Menem wrote, "For this purpose we will spend 600 million pesos (one peso=one dollar) provided by the World Bank."

The president promised not only money for the poor, but also harsh justice for violent demonstrators, whom he accused of "sheltering behind the weak whilst seeking the intervention of state security forces so that they can then shout out indignantly against " indiscriminate repression."
Menem blamed the current 17.3 percent unemployment rate on old policies of previous governments which gave "artificial occupation to tens of thousands of people."
